source.title: Indian Polity (question set written from its topics)

chapter.name: Historical Background
chapter.blurb: The Company Rule (1773-1858) and the Crown Rule (1858-1947): the Acts that shaped India's constitutional framework.

concepts.name: The Company Rule (1773-1858): Regulating Act 1773 to the Act of 1786
concepts.description: How Parliament first regulated the East India Company through the Acts of 1773, 1781, 1784 and 1786.
concepts.idea: Britain gradually brought the Company's political power under Parliament's control between 1773 and 1786.
concepts.rule: The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first step by which the British Government controlled the Company. It made the Governor of Bengal the Governor-General of Bengal, with an executive council of four, and Warren Hastings was the first holder. It made Bombay and Madras subordinate to Bengal and set up a Supreme Court at Calcutta in 1774. The Amending Act of 1781 (Act of Settlement) exempted the Governor-General and his council, and the Company's servants, from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction for official acts and excluded revenue matters. Pitt's India Act of 1784 separated commercial from political functions: the Court of Directors handled trade and a new Board of Control handled political affairs, giving a system of double government. The Act of 1786 was passed because Cornwallis, as Governor-General, wanted the power to override his council and to be Commander-in-Chief.
concepts.example: The Board of Control of 1784 supervised the Company's civil, military and revenue affairs for the Crown.

concepts.name: The Charter Acts of 1793, 1813, 1833 and 1853
concepts.description: The renewals of the Company's charter and what each changed: monopoly, sovereignty, centralisation and the legislative council.
concepts.idea: The Charter Acts moved from renewing the Company's trade monopoly to centralised rule and a separate legislative council.
concepts.rule: The Charter Act of 1793 extended the overriding power of Cornwallis to all future Governors-General and Governors, extended the trade monopoly by twenty years and made the Board of Control's members and staff payable from Indian revenues. The Charter Act of 1813 abolished the Company's trade monopoly except in tea and trade with China, asserted the sovereignty of the Crown over Company territories, allowed Christian missionaries and provided for western education. The Charter Act of 1833 was the final step to centralisation: it made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India, with Lord William Bentinck the first, ended the Company's commercial role, and took away legislative power from Bombay and Madras. The Charter Act of 1853 separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's council, added six legislative councillors, introduced open competition for the civil service and led to the Macaulay Committee (1854).
concepts.example: Under the 1833 Act, laws made by the Governor-General were called Acts, unlike earlier Regulations.

concepts.name: The Crown Rule begins: Acts of 1858, 1861 and 1892
concepts.description: The transfer of power to the Crown after 1857 and the first steps towards association of Indians with law-making.
concepts.idea: After the Revolt of 1857 the Crown took over from the Company and slowly began to associate Indians with legislation.
concepts.rule: The Government of India Act of 1858, passed after the Revolt of 1857, abolished the East India Company and transferred power to the Crown. It changed the Governor-General's title to Viceroy, and Lord Canning became the first Viceroy. It abolished the Board of Control and Court of Directors, ending double government, created the office of Secretary of State for India, a member of the British Cabinet, and a 15-member Council of India as an advisory body. The Indian Councils Act of 1861 began representative institutions by allowing the Viceroy to nominate non-official Indians, restored legislative powers to Bombay and Madras (decentralisation), recognised the portfolio system and allowed the Viceroy to issue ordinances lasting six months. The Indian Councils Act of 1892 increased the non-official members, allowed discussion of the budget and questions to the executive, and provided for nomination on the recommendation of bodies, a limited and indirect use of election.
concepts.example: In 1862 Lord Canning nominated three Indians to his legislative council.

concepts.name: The Morley-Minto Reforms 1909 and the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms 1919
concepts.description: Communal electorates, Indian members in executive councils, dyarchy and bicameralism.
concepts.idea: The 1909 Act expanded councils and separate electorates; the 1919 Act introduced dyarchy and a bicameral central legislature.
concepts.rule: The Indian Councils Act of 1909, or Morley-Minto Reforms, raised the Central legislative council from 16 to 60 members, kept an official majority at the Centre but allowed non-official majorities in the provinces, and allowed supplementary questions and budget resolutions. Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first Indian on the Viceroy's executive council as Law Member. It introduced separate electorates for Muslims, so Lord Minto is called the Father of Communal Electorate. The Government of India Act of 1919, or Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, followed the 1917 declaration of responsible government as the aim. It divided subjects into central and provincial under Devolution Rules and divided provincial subjects into transferred (public health, education, local government, agriculture) and reserved (police, justice, prisons, land revenue, finance). This was dyarchy. It introduced bicameralism (Council of State and Legislative Assembly) with direct elections, required three of six executive council members to be Indian, extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans, created the High Commissioner for India in London, set up a Public Service Commission (Central, 1926), separated provincial budgets and created a Chamber of Princes.
concepts.example: Education and public health were transferred subjects, while police and justice were reserved.

concepts.name: The Simon Commission, Communal Award and Poona Pact
concepts.description: The statutory commission of 1927, the Round Table Conferences, the Communal Award of 1932 and the Poona Pact.
concepts.idea: The Simon Commission, the Communal Award and the Poona Pact shaped the 1935 Act.
concepts.rule: In November 1927 the British Government appointed a seven-member statutory commission under Sir John Simon to report on the working of the 1919 Act, two years before schedule. All members were British, so parties boycotted it. Its 1930 report recommended abolition of dyarchy, extension of responsible government in the provinces, a federation of British India and princely states, and continuation of communal electorates. Three Round Table Conferences followed, then a White Paper, and the recommendations of the Joint Select Committee were included in the Act of 1935. In August 1932 Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award, which continued separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans and extended them to the depressed classes. Gandhiji undertook a fast unto death at Yerawada Jail. The Poona Pact between the Congress and Dr B.R. Ambedkar kept the Hindu joint electorate and gave reserved seats to the depressed classes.
concepts.example: The Poona Pact provisions were later incorporated in the 1935 Act.

concepts.name: The Government of India Act 1935 and the Indian Independence Act 1947
concepts.description: The federation, provincial autonomy and other features of 1935, and the partition and dominion provisions of 1947.
concepts.idea: The 1935 Act planned a federation and gave provincial autonomy; the 1947 Act ended British rule and created two dominions.
concepts.rule: The Government of India Act of 1935 was a long document with 321 sections and 10 schedules. It proposed an All-India Federation of provinces and princely states, divided powers into a Federal List (59 items), Provincial List (54) and Concurrent List (36) with residuary powers to the Viceroy, but the federation never came into being because the princely states did not join. It abolished dyarchy in the provinces and introduced provincial autonomy, effective in 1937 and discontinued in 1939, and provided for dyarchy at the Centre, which never came into operation. It introduced bicameralism in six of eleven provinces, reserved seats for the depressed classes and extended special representation to women and labour, abolished the Council of India and extended the franchise to about 14 per cent of the population. It established a Reserve Bank of India, a Federal Public Service Commission, provincial and joint commissions, and a Federal Court in 1937. The Indian Independence Act of 1947 declared India independent from 15 August 1947, created two dominions, India and Pakistan, and ended the office of the Viceroy and the Secretary of State for India.
concepts.example: Provincial autonomy under the 1935 Act was in force from 1937 to 1939.
